_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in a download menu and a docs banner, not in
a document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` drives an automatic warning on the website and in the docs. Set it true when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`, and say so in the first highlight.
highlights: A plain helm upgrade from v0.12.x: no migration, and no API, topic, permission or configuration change.

Geofence limits are now part of a tenant's plan. The limit on positions in one fence and the limit on fences per tenant are tier settings rather than fixed numbers, joined by a new limit on the total positions across a tenant's whole fence set. All three keep their previous values by default, so a tenant nobody has changed is metered exactly where it was.
A change is refused only when it makes one of those numbers larger. Lowering a tenant's limits never strands the fences it already holds, and renaming or deleting a fence keeps working regardless.

Large fence sets now hold together on the wire. A fence's shape is stored once and addressed by its content, and the detection engine is handed a list of references rather than every shape inline — so a fence set no longer has to fit in one broker message, and editing one fence no longer rewrites the rest.

Geofencing does less work per event: deciding that a device is outside a fence is now roughly seventy times cheaper, and an edit that changes only a fence's name no longer republishes the whole set to the engine.
Dependency and base-image updates across the Go modules and the web console, plus a contrast fix for control borders in the console.
